0.1.goal: Summarise one class's 30 test scores two ways: describe the class you have, then infer a plausible range for the wider group.

blocks.title: Enter the 30 test scores
blocks.text: The teacher's 30 end-of-term scores, held in a NumPy array. The mean is 74 and the standard deviation about 12.3, as in the lesson.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

scores = np.array([41,57,61,62,62,62,65,65,68,68,70,72,72,73,73,75,75,76,77,77,78,79,80,84,86,86,88,95,95,98])

print('students:', len(scores))
print('lowest to highest:', scores.min(), 'to', scores.max())

blocks.title: Describe: summarise what we have
blocks.text: Descriptive statistics only talk about these 30 students. The mean and median give the centre, and the standard deviation (ddof=1, the sample version) gives the typical distance from the average.
blocks.code:
mean = scores.mean()
median = np.median(scores)
sd = scores.std(ddof=1)

print(f'mean   = {mean:.1f}')
print(f'median = {median:.1f}')
print(f'sd     = {sd:.1f}')
print(f'about 2/3 of scores lie within {mean - sd:.1f} to {mean + sd:.1f}')

blocks.title: Infer: a 95% confidence interval
blocks.text: Now treat the 30 students as a sample from a bigger group. stats.t.interval gives a range of plausible values for that group's true mean. The standard error (sd divided by the square root of n) says how much a mean of 30 scores wobbles.
blocks.code:
n = len(scores)
se = sd / np.sqrt(n)

low, high = stats.t.interval(0.95, df=n - 1, loc=mean, scale=se)

print(f'standard error = {se:.2f}')
print(f'95% CI for the true mean: ({low:.1f}, {high:.1f})')

blocks.title: What each one tells you
blocks.text: The describing numbers are exact facts about these 30 scores. The interval is an estimate about people we did not test, and it comes with stated uncertainty. That is the whole difference between the two branches.
blocks.code:
print('DESCRIBE: this class averaged', round(mean, 1), 'with a typical spread of', round(sd, 1))
print('INFER: a wider group of similar students probably averages between', round(low, 1), 'and', round(high, 1))
print('Is the interval narrower than the spread of scores?', (high - low) < 2 * sd)

r.expect: mean 74; median 74; sd 12.29; 95 percent confidence interval: 69.41 to 78.59
r.note: sd() in R is the sample version (divides by n - 1), the same as ddof=1. t.test(scores) is used here only to get the 95% interval for the mean.

spss.syntax:
DATA LIST FREE / score.
BEGIN DATA
41 57 61 62 62 62 65 65 68 68 70 72 72 73 73 75 75 76 77 77 78 79 80 84 86 86 88 95 95 98
END DATA.
EXAMINE VARIABLES=score
  /PLOT=NONE
  /STATISTICS=DESCRIPTIVES
  /CINTERVAL 95.
spss.note: The Descriptives table shows the mean with its 95% confidence interval, the median, the standard deviation, the minimum and the maximum together.

stata.code:
clear
set obs 30
generate score = real(word("41 57 61 62 62 62 65 65 68 68 70 72 72 73 73 75 75 76 77 77 78 79 80 84 86 86 88 95 95 98", _n))
summarize score, detail
ci means score
stata.note: The word() line is a compact way to type 30 numbers. summarize, detail gives the mean, median (the 50% row) and standard deviation (sample version). ci means gives the mean with its 95% confidence interval.

try: Make the sample smaller by keeping only the first 10 scores. Predict whether the 95% interval gets wider or narrower, then run it.
Change 0.95 to 0.99 in stats.t.interval. Predict what happens to the width of the interval.

0.2.goal: Build a small student table with a nominal, an ordinal, a discrete and a continuous column, and see which summaries make sense for each.

blocks.title: Build a table with four kinds of data
blocks.text: One column per type: eye colour (nominal), grade level (ordinal, so we tell pandas the order), siblings (discrete, counted) and height (continuous, measured). The dtypes show how pandas stores each one.
blocks.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    'eye': ['brown','blue','brown','green','brown','blue','hazel','brown','green','blue'],
    'grade': ['Sophomore','Senior','Freshman','Junior','Sophomore','Senior','Freshman','Sophomore','Junior','Senior'],
    'siblings': [1, 0, 2, 3, 1, 1, 0, 2, 4, 1],
    'height_cm': [172.4, 165.1, 180.3, 158.9, 175.6, 169.8, 162.2, 177.0, 171.3, 183.5],
})
df['eye'] = df['eye'].astype('category')
df['grade'] = pd.Categorical(df['grade'],
    categories=['Freshman','Sophomore','Junior','Senior'], ordered=True)
print(df.dtypes)

blocks.title: Count the categories
blocks.text: For categories the natural summary is a count (or a percentage), not an average. value_counts does it. With sort=False the ordinal column stays in its natural order, from Freshman to Senior.
blocks.code:
print(df['eye'].value_counts())
print()
print(df['grade'].value_counts(sort=False))
print()
print('share Junior or above:', (df['grade'] >= 'Junior').mean())

blocks.title: Describe the numbers
blocks.text: Counts and measurements are real amounts, so mean, standard deviation and quartiles all make sense. describe gives them in one table.

blocks.title: Why averaging a category makes no sense
blocks.text: Pandas refuses to average a category. If you force it by turning grades into codes 1 to 4, you get a number like 2.6 that is not a grade, and it pretends the gaps between grades are equal. For an ordinal column use counts, the maximum or a share instead.

r.code:
eye <- factor(c('brown','blue','brown','green','brown','blue','hazel','brown','green','blue'))
grade <- factor(c('Sophomore','Senior','Freshman','Junior','Sophomore','Senior','Freshman','Sophomore','Junior','Senior'),
  levels = c('Freshman','Sophomore','Junior','Senior'), ordered = TRUE)
siblings <- c(1, 0, 2, 3, 1, 1, 0, 2, 4, 1)
height_cm <- c(172.4, 165.1, 180.3, 158.9, 175.6, 169.8, 162.2, 177.0, 171.3, 183.5)
table(eye)
table(grade)
summary(siblings)
summary(height_cm)
mean(eye)
r.expect: eye: blue 3, brown 4, green 2, hazel 1; grade: Freshman 2, Sophomore 3, Junior 2, Senior 3; siblings mean 1.5; height_cm mean 171.61; mean(eye) gives NA with a warning
r.note: R lists the eye colours alphabetically, while pandas lists them by size. mean(eye) returns NA with a warning, R's way of refusing to average a category.

spss.menu: Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Frequencies (categories) and Descriptives (numbers)
spss.syntax:
DATA LIST FREE / eye (A6) grade siblings height.
BEGIN DATA
brown 2 1 172.4 blue 4 0 165.1 brown 1 2 180.3 green 3 3 158.9 brown 2 1 175.6
blue 4 1 169.8 hazel 1 0 162.2 brown 2 2 177.0 green 3 4 171.3 blue 4 1 183.5
END DATA.
VALUE LABELS grade 1 'Freshman' 2 'Sophomore' 3 'Junior' 4 'Senior'.
VARIABLE LEVEL eye (NOMINAL) /grade (ORDINAL) /siblings height (SCALE).
FREQUENCIES VARIABLES=eye grade.
DESCRIPTIVES VARIABLES=siblings height.
spss.note: SPSS stores grade as codes 1 to 4 with labels. VARIABLE LEVEL tells SPSS each column's measurement level; use Frequencies for the two categories and Descriptives for the two numbers.

stata.code:
clear
set obs 10
generate eye = word("brown blue brown green brown blue hazel brown green blue", _n)
generate grade = real(word("2 4 1 3 2 4 1 2 3 4", _n))
generate siblings = real(word("1 0 2 3 1 1 0 2 4 1", _n))
generate height = real(word("172.4 165.1 180.3 158.9 175.6 169.8 162.2 177.0 171.3 183.5", _n))
label define g 1 "Freshman" 2 "Sophomore" 3 "Junior" 4 "Senior"
label values grade g
tabulate eye
tabulate grade
summarize siblings height
stata.note: Stata keeps the ordinal grade as codes 1 to 4 with value labels. tabulate counts categories, and summarize is for numbers only.

0.3.goal: See that a sample statistic wanders around the fixed population parameter, that bigger samples wander less, and that a biased sample does not.

blocks.title: The lesson's ten shops
blocks.text: Here the population is small enough to see: monthly sales of 10 shops. The population mean (a parameter) is fixed. Each sample of 3 shops gives a different sample mean (a statistic). The population SD divides by N (ddof=0), the sample SD by n - 1 (ddof=1).
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

shops = np.array([12, 15, 9, 22, 18, 7, 25, 14, 20, 11])
mu = shops.mean()
print(f'population mean (mu) = {mu:.2f}, sigma = {shops.std(ddof=0):.3f}')

samples = {'A': shops[[0, 3, 5]], 'B': shops[[6, 4, 1]], 'C': shops[[2, 9, 7]]}
for name, s in samples.items():
    print(f'sample {name}: {s}  x-bar = {s.mean():.2f}  gap = {s.mean() - mu:+.2f}')
print(f'sample A sd = {samples["A"].std(ddof=1):.3f}')

blocks.title: A bigger, seeded population
blocks.text: Now a population of 10,000 weekly study times in hours, made with a fixed seed so everyone gets the same numbers. We pretend not to know its mean and compute it once: this is the parameter.
blocks.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
population = rng.normal(loc=14, scale=4, size=10_000).round(1)

mu = population.mean()
print('population size N =', len(population))
print(f'population mean mu = {mu:.3f}')

blocks.title: Sampling error shrinks as n grows
blocks.text: For each sample size we draw one random sample and show its gap from mu. Then we repeat the draw 300 times to see the typical gap. Bigger samples miss by less. The gap never vanishes completely: that is sampling error, and it is normal.
blocks.code:
for n in [10, 50, 250, 1000]:
    one = rng.choice(population, size=n, replace=False).mean()
    many = [rng.choice(population, size=n, replace=False).mean() for _ in range(300)]
    typical = np.mean(np.abs(np.array(many) - mu))
    print(f'n = {n:4d}: one sample mean = {one:6.2f}, typical gap over 300 samples = {typical:.3f}')

blocks.title: A biased sample does not get better
blocks.text: Suppose we only ask the 1,000 heaviest studiers (say, people we meet in the library). Even with a large sample the mean stays far from mu, because the method is tilted. A bigger sample cannot fix bias.
blocks.code:
top = np.sort(population)[-1000:]

for n in [10, 100, 1000]:
    m = rng.choice(top, size=n, replace=False).mean()
    print(f'biased sample n = {n:4d}: mean = {m:.2f}, gap from mu = {m - mu:+.2f}')

r.code:
shops <- c(12, 15, 9, 22, 18, 7, 25, 14, 20, 11)
mean(shops)
sqrt(mean((shops - mean(shops))^2))
A <- shops[c(1, 4, 6)]
mean(A)
sd(A)
mean(shops[c(7, 5, 2)])
mean(shops[c(3, 10, 8)])
r.expect: mu 15.3; population sigma 5.551; sample A mean 13.67, sd 7.638; sample B mean 19.33; sample C mean 11.33
r.note: R, SPSS and Stata have no population SD command, so R uses the formula directly. Random draws would differ from Python's because each program has its own random numbers, so we use the lesson's fixed samples.

spss.syntax:
DATA LIST FREE / sales inA.
BEGIN DATA
12 1 15 0 9 0 22 1 18 0
7 1 25 0 14 0 20 0 11 0
END DATA.
DESCRIPTIVES VARIABLES=sales.
TEMPORARY.
SELECT IF (inA = 1).
DESCRIPTIVES VARIABLES=sales.
spss.note: The first table shows mu = 15.3 for all 10 shops. The second, for sample A only, shows x-bar = 13.67 and SD 7.638. SPSS always gives the sample SD (n - 1), so for all 10 shops it shows 5.851, not the population 5.551.

stata.code:
clear
set obs 10
generate sales = real(word("12 15 9 22 18 7 25 14 20 11", _n))
generate inA = inlist(_n, 1, 4, 6)
summarize sales
summarize sales if inA == 1
stata.note: The first summarize gives mu = 15.3 for all shops, the second gives x-bar = 13.67 and SD 7.638 for sample A. Stata's SD is always the sample version, so for all 10 shops it shows 5.851.
